item.title: Salvaging that which is dearest
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: In the midst of this turmoil, we attempt to make sense of it all by trying to salvage what is dearest to us. This post is about what I instinctively rushed to salvage, what appears to be dearest to me as a mathematician
item.content:encoded:
David Cimasoni, senior lecturer at University of Geneva

AI use: none. See the last footnote of this post.

My emotional state during the past months may best be described as passing through the five stages of grief – every single week. However, it was also heartening to discover the numerous beautiful and inspiring essays written by fellow mathematicians. I frequently experience positive emotions reading them, including a sense of community belonging which is stronger than ever. It seems that dealing collectively with grief provides many of us with a genuine bonding experience.

I also find it poignant to see how, in the midst of such turmoil, we attempt to make sense of it all by trying to salvage what is dearest to us. High profile mathematicians often eloquently advocate preserving the “artisanal way” of research which played such an important role in making them who they are, while passionate instructors primarily focus on how best to reform curriculums in order to address the challenges of the new era. As for junior mathematicians, they frequently embrace the new tools to keep alive their dream of a successful career in academia – and understandably so.

This post1 is about what, to my own surprise, I instinctively rushed to salvage, what appears to be dearest to me as a mathematician. Its aim is not so much to contribute to a debate, but rather to elicit the same kind of emotion I experienced myself while reading other contributions to this remarkable platform.

Disclaimer

I am blessed with an academic position among the least impacted by the AI revolution: high enough not to worry about my professional future (aka tenured), and low enough to experience neither dramatic loss of status nor constant fear of being scooped.2 From this advantageous situation, it is not too difficult for me to adopt a relatively positive tone for this note. This does not mean that I am unaware of the dire situations faced by many colleagues (especially junior ones), and that I do not deeply care about them.

Societal impact of the AI revolution

Like many others, my first reaction in trying to make sense of the rapid societal changes is to reach for historical parallels and analogies.

Similarly to the industrial and agricultural revolutions which gave us access to unimaginable amounts of physical power and nutrients, generative AI tools provide us with direct access to “answers” that were beforehand only available via (at least some minimal amount of) personal reflexion. Just as it is now widely accepted that regularly using one’s physical power is a good idea and binging on food is not,
it seems crucial to understand the importance of following a balanced “AI diet”3. Those who fail to do so face the danger of a rapid loss of cognitive well-being, a deskilling incomparably more rapid and brutal than those induced by the industrial and agricultural revolutions.4

Reaching for another analogy, I tend to think that AI tools are to intelligence what social media are to socialization. While Facebook and Instagram made us globally more connected, it is doubtful that many of us actually became more social in the process. Similarly, while ChatGPT and Claude might well allow for spectacular collective progress with respect to specific goals, I do not believe that it is making any of us smarter – rather the opposite.

There is a real risk that new generations will fail to put in the hard graft necessary to develop their cognitive abilities, reaching adulthood with their pockets full of answers but with little intellectual rigor, critical thinking, etc. In this new era where answers are available at our fingertips, it is crucial to insist on the fundamental right to make mistakes. Quoting Grothendieck:

To fear the error and to fear the truth are one and the same.
One who fears to be wrong is powerless to discover.5

Delivering these messages is most probably one of the greatest contemporary challenges faced by parents and teachers. Hopefully, this will allow us to refocus education on its primary goal: teaching how to think independently without taking answers at face value, whether it comes from a friend, a parent, a professor, a politician seeking reelection, or an LLM. The stakes for our democratic societies are difficult to overestimate.

Even more fundamentally, the emergence of these tools brings to the forefront the philosophical question of the intrinsic value of an activity, since AI can more often than not carry it out on our behalf. Nowadays, it is certainly possible to ask ChatGPT to chose the birthday gift of one’s child and to write the card – this does not mean that it is a good idea. Similarly, immediately asking Claude for the answer to a given question will often defeat the purpose (which is to think about the question rather than to obtain the answer), just like taking a helicopter defeats the purpose of a mountain hike.

Societal role of mathematicians in the AI revolution

How can I, as a mathematician, be useful in trying to address the challenges of the ongoing revolution?

Since “hallucinations” can be filtered out more efficiently in our field than in any other, it has been argued that mathematics could be used to supply “theoretical upper bound for what the maximal safe level of AI use can be”. I disagree: this bound is extremely high, and therefore of no practical value whatsoever. Mathematics could once again6 provide a false impression of rigour and security regarding the application of these tools to the fields they will inevitably tackle in the future.

On the other hand, I see three reasons why mathematics constitutes the ideal discipline to help us all face the societal impact of the AI revolution.

The first reason is obvious: mathematics is par excellence a human activity which strengthens cognitive reflexion. Here is the second: formal mathematical language upholds the highest standards of clarity, rigour, and precision – the ideal framework for conducting a healthy debate. Thurston formulates this beautifully in his famous essay:

Because we have a high standard for clear and convincing thinking and because we place a high value on listening to and trying to understand each other, we don’t engage in interminable arguments and endless redoing of our mathematics. We are prepared to be convinced by others.

Research in cognitive psychology conducted during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic precisely identified these two criteria (scoring high at cognitive reflexion and low at socio-cognitive polarisation) as the most heavily correlated with the ability to discern real or fake news. In times of uncertainty, mathematics therefore constitutes a field of the utmost importance to help us become enlightened citizens.7

The third reason why I believe that mathematics forms a crucial part of the solution to the societal challenges of AI lies in the true goal of our discipline. As passionately explained by many, the product of mathematics is neither proofs nor theorems, but human understanding, which will always remain the prerogative of human beings.8 For an honest description of our raison d’être, we absolutely need to articulate the neuroplastic value of intelligibility. And once again, it is on Thurston’s shoulders that I like to stand to do so, via his famous post9 on MathOverflow:

It’s not mathematics that you need to contribute to. It’s deeper than that: how might you contribute to humanity, and even deeper, to the well-being of the world, by pursuing mathematics? (...…) The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves. Is there, for example any real reason that even such famous results as Fermat’s Last Theorem, or the Poincaré conjecture, really matter? Their real importance is not in their specific statements, but their role in challenging our understanding, presenting challenges that led to mathematical developments that
increased our understanding. The world does not suffer from an oversupply of clarity and understanding (to put it mildly).

Afterword

In 1994, I had proudly announced to my neighbour that I was about to undertake studies in mathematics. His reply had amused me quite a bit: “But mathematics is useless nowadays, with computers!” It was easy to laugh about it thirty years ago – less so today.

As late as March 2026, I was still claiming that while translators and programmers would rapidly become obsolete, the activity of mathematical research still had a bright future ahead and would certainly be the last one impacted...… Yes, I lingered in the first stage of grief for longer than I would like to admit. I now realise that this delusion was rooted in an inappropriate feeling of superiority: the AI revolution has forced upon me a lesson in humility that was probably long overdue.

I feel extremely fortunate to have secured a stable professional position before the advent of these new tools. This allows me to make a free choice about their use10 without fear for my own future. But I do fear for the future of my children.

Given the revolution unfolding before our eyes and the threats it poses to our democratic societies, it is legitimate to ask how our skills might best be put to use. As a mathematician, how should I devote my efforts to the “well-being of the world“? Should the priority be to broaden our individual and collective understanding of the world through research? Or should it rather be to help the next generations choose the path of cognitive independence, of intellectual rigour, and of questioning their own beliefs? Of course, the two are not mutually exclusive, and the abilities required are not interchangeable. Yet, in light of my personal competences and values, I find myself tempted to redirect a substantial portion of my energy from the former to the latter.

Only time will tell if this is just me dwelling in the third stage of grief.

Received 30 September 2026.

  1. It is loosely based on a more comprehensive essay (in French). ︎
  2. Anyone at an AI company trying to run its frontier model on the kind of questions I am currently pondering would probably get fired on the spot. ︎
  3. An expression coined by Tao for university students, but which applies to everybody. ︎
  4. Incidentally, the first (neolithic) agricultural revolution did not lead to a reduction in famines and malnutrition, and historians argue that it is not Homo sapiens that domesticated wheat but rather the other way around; this makes the analogy with the AI revolution all the more interesting. ︎
  5. Craindre l’erreur et craindre la vérité est une seule et même chose. Celui qui craint de se tromper est impuissant à découvrir. (English translation from this source.) ︎
  6. I am old enough to remember the role played by mathematics in the 2007 subprime mortgage crisis. ︎
  7. Plato has understood this fact, as mathematics and dialectic formed the core disciplines of his Academy. ︎
  8. A tautology that I find soothing. ︎
  9. A post written on the day of his 64th birthday, less than two years before his death. ︎
  10. In my research, but also elsewhere: no LLM was used in the production of this text (though thanks are due to Paul Turner for reviewing the language). ︎

item.title: Mathematics and mysticism: another defense of human mathematics
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: My intention here is to contribute to the discussion by pointing at an aspect of mathematics which I believe is under threat and has been forgotten in the rubble of this ongoing earthquake: the mystical aspect of mathematics. I am aware that using the word “mystical” in the mathematics community comes with some risks; yet I will try to defend it, because I think that this is one of the crucial aspects of human engagement with mathematics.
item.content:encoded:
Ignacio Barros, Assistant Professor at University of Antwerp

Acknowledgments and AI Disclosure: No ai was used. In exchange for coffee, I lured my colleague Edward Bryden (a human!) into my office to check my text. He generously corrected it and made suggestions that resulted in a definite improvement. I have left some of my spanish influenced mistakes for expository proposes and to, again, keep writing human!

We have all witnessed how the arrival and display of power of a foreign technology, to be found a few years ago in Philip Dick novels, has forced us into a healthy and long due discussion about the purpose and future of our doing as mathematicians. The range of answers and public reactions has been rather motley, yet at times elitist and riddled with moralizing considerations on our shared responsibility. One hears from some that we are to maintain the human aspect of mathematics at all costs and from others that we have to accept the reality as it changes and keep mathematics engaged in a world where artificial intelligence dominates larger territories of human intellectuality. All voices come from our shared love for mathematics.

I am writing not to offer an alternative point of view, I am much too slow of a thinker to form an articulated standpoint regarding artificial intelligence in the middle of this very loud maelstrom. My mind goes immediately to Quino’s genius expressing what many of us feel now.

My intention here is to contribute to the discussion of an aspect of mathematics which I believe is under threat and has been forgotten in the rubble of this ongoing earthquake: the mystical aspect of mathematics. I am aware that using the word “mystical” in the mathematics community comes with some risks; yet I will try to defend it, because I think that this is one of the crucial aspects of human engagement with mathematics. Not only has it been there all along, certainly for the several thousand years of recorded mathematics, but it is in urgent need of protection from the settlers and their powerful machines.

We have fallen too easily into the comforting belief that science is a societal response to the human need for understanding the world, and that mathematics, as such, will never disappear. Even when the settlers and their machines are capable of answering all our questions, proving all our theorems, perhaps even formulating the questions, embarking on homeric research explorations and explaining their findings with soft patience and exemplary clarity, we say to ourselves, as long as we are humans, mathematics will not disappear because it comes from one of our defining ways to be in this world: trying to understand it. Our ways of doing mathematics might change, and perhaps the type of mathematics we do in the future will be reshaped, but our need for engaging with mathematics will always be there. As a warm someone in this blog offering comfort said: we can always take joy in the beauty of mathematics, independent of its creator. I agree with all this. Yet, just as our personal and communal relationship with the world is much more complex and mysterious than simply trying to understand it, the same is true for mathematics. In my eyes, it is a fatal mistake to cling to this optimistic premise and, to use the language of the settlers, wait until the sea is calm again and the machines open the way to a new era of mathematical research.

One could argue that the only other universal product of human culture present throughout our history that distinctly uses symbolism as much as we do in mathematics is our myths. Religion being the most prominent example. Although mathematics and myths use symbols in very different ways, it is not a coincidence that it is in these two places that we can find them sprouting from every branch. Religion accepts its relationship to the mystery, and it is perhaps because we want to mark some distance that we ignore the mystery in our doing.

We are not always aware of this, but whenever we write “Let X be a …\ldots ” we are doing something much deeper than just fixing a name for a mathematical object; we are spelling some form of life to a mind-conceived object, and once it has been spelled, we can observe it interact with us and with its peers. This points directly at our anemic, yet desperately human power of creation. This permeates our work, from leaders in our fields conceiving game changing mathematical constructions to small decorations on a lemma intended to help us overcome a harmless obstacle.

Creativity covers a large portion of our relationship to the world. We place creativity in the realm of intuition; reason and understanding are only there to shape, order, and filter, as clothes that wrap around them, giving shelter and warmth. Understanding comes after creating, yet both are needed, both drive us to do mathematics, and both are a deep and unavoidable response to our awe at being thrown into this world. The discourse that it doesn’t matter what creates new mathematics, as long as we as humans engage in appreciating and understanding it, is a fallacy. If it is not us the ones breathing life into our delicate, glacial, and often beautiful objects, then human mathematics dies. Maybe not in a decade, maybe not in a century, but eventually our creative pulsion will take us somewhere else.

We all know that academia has its fair share of big egos, but for the overwhelming majority of mathematicians, conjectures are there not to find heroism in solving them. They do play a central role in helping us orient ourselves and our research communities in our explorations of the ever growing landscape of mathematics. But this is not their only role. They also help us stay in contact, as a community, with the fact that we are part of a living mystery, and that no matter how far we go in our explorations, darkness, the unknown, the mystery is always around us. Conjectures are attractive and grounding because of this.

If you think about it, most of our time is spent in the unknown. Our most common state of mind is confusion, disorientation, and at times desperation. The goal of this never ending doing that we call mathematics is never to find comfort in the questions answered. We are almost allergic to that comfort. As soon as we get there, we move on as quickly as possible, we find the next mystery, we jump almost as a reaction into the darkness again. Why do we do this? I don’t think it is because we hopelessly suffer from the fever of “progress”, whose premise is that reality as it is needs to be changed as fast and as radically as possible. No, we have been doing mathematics for much longer than the rampant pandemic of progress. We do this because of our human need to collectively and individually stay in touch with that ancestral awe that made science and mathematics possible, to remind us that our place in this world is not under the encandilating light of answers, but rather under the dim light over the space between the answers and complete darkness.

Someone please tell the settlers to use their machines for something else!

Ignacio Barros,
September 29, 2026.

Received 29 September 2026.

item.title: Use LLMs to check your work
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Most discussions about LLMs in mathematics seem to focus on their (rapidly advancing) proof discovery abilities and the effects these abilities may have on professional mathematics. I write here about a different use of these technologies, to make the following point: we have a professional duty to use LLMs to proofread our work.
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

AI disclosure. This essay was composed on the Notes app of the author’s iPhone. This app provides AI assistance with spelling, grammar, and auto-completion of words being typed.

Most discussions about LLMs in mathematics seem to focus on their (rapidly advancing) proof discovery abilities and the effects these abilities may have on professional mathematics. I write here about a different use of these technologies, to make the following point: we have a professional duty to use LLMs to proofread our work. I use “proofread” to mean both copy editing of no mathematical substance, as well as the detection and correction of mathematical errors and gaps in arguments. By “our work,” I mean our research papers, though the arguments below extend with straightforward modifications to teaching materials.

First, a fundamental community norm is that we should make all reasonable efforts to ensure that our proofs are correct. Modern LLMs are tools that, when used appropriately, can provide this assurance with high confidence and little effort.

Second, incorrect or inadequately justified proofs exact a substantial human cost. I have refereed many papers in my career; the vast majority had at least some minor mathematical issues, and a not insignificant minority had issues that required new contributions by the author(s) to patch. Identifying these issues and writing a detailed referee report to alert the author(s) takes many hours, especially for long and technical papers.

Before LLMs, I executed my referee responsibilities with pride, knowing that authors were (typically) putting forth the best work they could, and that operating on the frontier of mathematical knowledge would inevitably involve some mistakes. Now, however, when I see clear mistakes in papers I am reviewing, I just feel disrespected. The author(s) had a tool they could have used to eliminate the mistakes and did not, wasting my time. (Certainly, LLMs are not perfect, but it is easy to tell when a cursory check has not been done.)

Recent events in my personal life have emphasized for me the value and precariousness of human life, and how death and life-limiting illness can strike unpredictably. Submitting work that has not gone through an LLM check to a journal may cost a conscientious referee many hours of their time. To ask someone to spend their most precious resource correcting errors that could have been caught with the push of a button is both rude and professionally negligent.

Some may argue that abstention from LLM checking is justified on ethical grounds. If this objection rests on the behavior of frontier labs, one can simply use open-weight models. If the objection rests on resource use, a simple calculation shows that the resource use from a few minutes of LLM computation pales in comparison to other activities we regularly undertake to advance mathematics, such as conference travel. I am sure there will be other creative objections, but it is hard for me to see how they can outweigh the cost refereeing erroneous mathematics has on human life (especially in combination with the cost to all other readers who might be interested in the result).

I also believe we have a duty to use LLMs for literature searches, to ensure correct attribution, and to make sure our arguments are as simple and straightforward as possible. The reasons are similar.

Received 30 September 2026.

item.title: Disadvantages of Designating Mathematicians for AI Output Releases
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “In our September 29 recommendations, we outlined an approach to the release of AI-generated mathematical output by AI labs. Since then, we have been asked by people from multiple labs and by several mathematicians about a specific aspect of the recommendations — that the development of human understanding following a release must remain organic and community led — and what it says about the question of the labs choosing specific mathematicians to participate in various ways in the release of their output. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence1, cross-posted at agmai.org

In our September 29 recommendations, we outlined an approach to the release of AI-generated mathematical output by AI labs. Since then, we have been asked by people from multiple labs and by several mathematicians about a specific aspect of the recommendations — that the development of human understanding following a release must remain organic and community led — and what it says about the question of the labs choosing specific mathematicians to participate in various ways in the release of their output. The purpose of this document is to clarify this point and to explain the reasoning behind our position on it. We welcome further feedback from the community and engagement with these arguments.

In some past releases an AI company has designated mathematicians to receive the output on a problem, often before anyone else. Those mathematicians then worked to uncover the ideas in the output, check them, develop them, and present them to the wider community. The appeal of this release model is easy to see: it puts expert eyes on the output early, can lead to a better initial public writeup, and gives each result a knowledgeable point of contact.

After consideration of many negative effects that this release plan has, however, we have come to the conclusion that on balance the disadvantages outweigh the advantages. This should in no way be construed as criticism of the mathematicians who have taken on such a role: they have acted in good faith and done valuable work. Nonetheless, we recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice for future releases, for the reasons below.

Delayed or unequal access. In cases where designated mathematicians see material before everyone else, they get a head start on problems others may have worked on for years. Other mathematicians may have valuable contributions to make based on the material but may not have access to it, and may be dissuaded from working on it.

The remaining reasons apply even if all the material is released publicly at once.

Denied agency. The choice of who works to understand, check, and write up an important AI-generated result is consequential, both for those chosen and for the field, especially in the current period of transition when norms around credit for mathematical activities are in flux. If an AI company designates a particular mathematician to undertake or lead this task, it is to an extent making this decision for the community and denying it agency over its field of study. Further, this choice may discourage other mathematicians from contributing to the understanding of the results.

Biased selection. Any choice of designated mathematicians by the AI companies reflects their networks and priorities, which are different from those of the mathematical community. However carefully the choice is made, it is opaque and unaccountable. Moreover, this practice could incentivize mathematicians to align with whatever they perceive the AI companies’ priorities to be.

Borrowed reputation. In practice, designated mathematicians’ names end up vouching for the release and shielding the AI company from criticism. Given the wide range of views on the release of results by companies in the mathematical community, that puts the designated mathematicians in a difficult position that could compromise their role of helping with understanding.

It is unnecessary. Recent experience has shown that human understanding can develop organically and efficiently when AI-generated material is made available. In many cases recently, mathematicians have independently read released AI output, worked to understand it, and written useful papers providing clear arguments that solve the problems. We are also aware of several reading groups, workshops and websites being organized to understand other AI-generated output, and there are new funding opportunities for such activities.

What we recommend instead

We recommend that any lab releasing AI-generated mathematical output should follow either pathway 2A of our recommendations (for scholarly articles produced by AI lab employees, adhering to standards set by the mathematical community) or pathway 2B (for unfinished products that the employees do not intend to write up as scholarly articles). A brief summary of pathway 2B is:

  1. AI labs should make a serious good faith effort to improve citations and exposition, including scouring the literature for any ideas that should be cited.
  2. Products should be posted on scholarly repositories that are not controlled by the posting AI lab, have citable identifiers, and record modifications.
  3. Products should be accompanied by information about the process that produced them: the name of the model, prompts, chains of thought, number of attempts, compute used, and costs.
  4. Proofs should be Lean-formalized where possible, unless it leads to unacceptable delays. Formalization artifacts should meet several community standards.
  5. AI labs should state how the problems were chosen and how many problems were attempted.
  6. AI companies should provide support, including funding, for the development of human understanding of the released products through academic workshops, working groups, and other activities. Decisions about which particular efforts are supported should be taken neither by AGMAI nor by AI companies, but by separate, independent nonprofit institutions.

Full details of our recommendations are provided in our September 29 recommendations. We recall that our recommendations are intended for mathematics, and not necessarily for other areas of science.

Received 25 October 2026.

  1. Members of the Advisory Group, as listed on agmai.org: François Charles (ENS-PSL), Camillo De Lellis (IAS, GSSI), Timothy Gowers (Collège de France, Cambridge), Martin Hairer (EPFL, Imperial College London), Nikhil Srivastava (Berkeley, Simons Institute), Ulrike Tillmann (Oxford), Ravi Vakil (Stanford), Edward Witten (IAS), Melanie Matchett Wood (Harvard). ︎

item.title: Could AI help correct the mathematical literature?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “We mathematicians know that published papers and books often contain mistakes: sometimes small, like a missing hypothesis or a wrong constant, and sometimes more serious, like a theorem that is false as stated. We are kind of used to this. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Alonso Castillo-Ramirez, Professor and Researcher at Universidad de Guadalajara

Disclosure: AI was used to assist with the writing and spell checking of this post. All the ideas are the author’s own, who takes full responsibility for them.

We mathematicians know that published papers and books often contain mistakes: sometimes small, like a missing hypothesis or a wrong constant, and sometimes more serious, like a theorem that is false as stated. We are kind of used to this. However, these mistakes are rarely corrected in public: the paper stays as it is, and the correction lives in the folklore of the community.

Over the last few months, I have used AI to check a few dozen published papers in research areas that I am interested in. In five of them, the AI flagged a mistake. I checked each flag myself, and all five were real.

As an example, a few weeks ago I asked ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to check our own 2023 paper “The relative rank of the endomorphism monoid of a finite G-set”, published in Semigroup Forum. The last section of this paper contains a subtle calculation, and for some time I have wondered whether it is entirely correct. The AI told me that the proof of Theorem 17 contains a mistake: we did not correctly describe the kernels of some G-equivariant transformations. It added that, with the correct description, the theorem still seems to hold.

In fact, my co-author and former PhD student, Ramón H. Ruiz-Medina, had pointed out the same problem to me a few months earlier, so the AI arrived on its own at something we already knew. It is unfortunate that the published proof has a mistake, but still, it gave me some peace of mind that the AI also believes the final calculation is correct.

This was a lucky case, since the mistake can be fixed. Not every case was like this: some of the mistakes the AI pointed out to me were real counterexamples to stated theorems.

For me, the main advantage of this approach is how little time and effort it takes to check a flag. If someone tells me that Lemma 3.2 fails for n = 2 and shows me why, I can verify it in a few minutes, whereas certifying every proof in a paper could take weeks.

The formalization community, including the Lean community, has argued for a long time that mathematical literature needs checking, and I fully agree. If we need to check every step, formalization is invaluable. But formalizing every single paper is slow and expensive, and in most cases a certificate is more than what we need.

Of course, my experiment is small. A few dozen papers is not much, and I do not know how many mistakes the AI missed in the papers where it found nothing. When the AI finds nothing, that does not mean the paper is correct, as it is far from being the same as a Lean certificate.

I am less sure what should happen after we find a mistake. Journals rarely publish corrections, and many mistakes that experts know about are never written down anywhere. It would be great to see a public record linked to each paper where anyone could look up the mistakes that have been reported, whether they have been confirmed, and whether they have been fixed.

The same kind of check could help before a paper is published. David Craven in his post “Where will all the papers go?” (Proofs and Prompts, Sep 19, 2026) argues that authors should run an LLM check before submitting a paper. I would go a step further: journals could offer an AI check at submission, with referees examining any concrete objections it raises. I think this could significantly reduce the number of published papers with mistakes in the future.

I do not plan to run a large project myself, but I think the idea deserves more attention. If you have used AI to check published papers, I would be interesting to hear about it. How many papers did you check, how many flags did you get, and how many were real mistakes?

Received 28 September 2026

item.title: Two technical questions: floating intellectual property and liability risks of AI agents and users in research
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: This was prompted by the recent disclosure that, in June 2026, an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI autonomously hacked into Australia's Medicare system to access non-public data.
item.content:encoded:
Pedro Freitas, Professor at Universidade de Lisboa

As it should be clear to all of us at this point, a large number of issues concerning the usage of AI in research need to be and are being discussed. While these cover an immensely varied spectrum, ranging from whether mathematicians should use it at all, to the environmental and social consequences using it will bring about, there are some technical points that, I believe, are relevant even if potentially not as important in the long run.

While some of the questions under discussion are fairly general in scope, a particular issue has recently been raised concerning the work around the counter-example for the Navier-Stokes equations. Shortly after OpenAI announced its AI agents had solved a version of the Navier-Stokes problem, concerns were raised regarding data privacy and intellectual property12. Further questions related to attribution have also been voiced, together with others about the way in which AI models make use of their interactions with mathematicians, and scientists in general.

Even if in this case suspicions were laid to rest – there are, as far as I know, no independent confirmations of this – the fact remains that once an idea is fed into a model (Check the viability of using technique T to solve problem P, for instance), it might become what may be described as floating in hyperspace. This means that, at least in theory, if another researcher asks the same AI model to solve problem P, they might be provided with the newly acquired idea of using technique T, which then goes from one human to another, without any of them being aware of this.

Similar problems were discussed at the 4th OECD Blue Sky Forum on science, technology and innovation data and indicators that took place in Paris in mid September. According to an article in Science Business, major funding agencies present at the meeting discussed “how they can stop confidential scientific ideas in grant proposals from leaking out through large language models (LLMs), for example if reviewers use AI to help them judge applications.” This may also be a problem should the candidates themselves write their applications with the help of a model.

There is, however, a scenario that I believe has not been mentioned explicitly so far, and which I find at least as worrying. This was prompted by the recent disclosure that, in June 2026, an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI autonomously hacked into Australia’s Medicare system to access non-public data. The Australian government was not notified of this breach until September, 84 days after the intrusion occurred3.

Apart from legal issues, which the Australian government states it is looking into, this incident poses the possibility that a swarm of autonomous AI agents, when tasked with solving a complex mathematical problem, like in the case of the Navier-Stokes equations, might attempt to hack into the computer of a mathematician known to be working at the forefront of that specific problem. While arguably less serious than a national health data breach, this would still be a considerable threat for science, particularly as it might never become known. Another possibility is that they try to break into a journal platform to check if there are relevant articles in that area under revision.

As some AI agents have already demonstrated their capability to work around security systems, mostly by brute-force but no less effective because of that, with the prompt at the origin of this behaviour being, in some sense, and for lack of a better word, innocent, the threats just described are no longer purely academic.

Again, should someone give an AI model a prompt or series of prompts to find the solution to a mathematical problem, it would seem that there is nothing stopping the model from trying to achieve its mission by carrying out actions that, if done by a human, would probably involve some legal consequences. Is this included in what researchers mean when they write what has become a standard sentence at the end of some AI disclosure sections of a paper, namely, that they take full responsibility for the results in the paper?

Summarising:

1. Is there invisible communication between different authors without their knowledge, even if privacy settings are on? In particular, can we be sure that agents do not hack their own system and collect information from interactions with other researchers?

2. Can we be sure that innocent prompts (solve problem X) will not cause agents to look for information in ways that are unlawful? Should that happen, which parties may be held legally responsible for any such actions?

  1. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/science/tristan-buckmaster-openai-math-navier-stokes.html ︎
  2. https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/sep/08/openai-claims-to-have-solved-maths-problem-that-stumped-humans-for-decades ︎
  3. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI_rogue_agent_breach_of_Medicare ︎
